drills.q: Name the three phases of a Lambda invocation and which one runs only once per execution environment.
drills.a: Download/INIT/INVOKE. INIT (runtime bootstrap plus global-scope code) runs once per execution environment lifetime; INVOKE runs the handler on every single call, warm or cold.

drills.q: Why does SnapStart take Java from 5+ seconds to under 150ms, mechanically?
drills.a: It snapshots the execution environment's memory and disk state AFTER init has already run once (JVM booted, classes loaded), caches that snapshot, and restores from it on subsequent cold starts instead of re-running the full JVM boot and class-loading sequence from scratch.

drills.q: A SnapStart-enabled function occasionally returns the same 'random' UUID across different cold starts. What's the bug?
drills.a: The UUID was generated during init and got frozen into the snapshot, so every cold start restored from that snapshot returns the same value. Fix: generate the UUID inside an afterRestore runtime hook (or per-invocation, not at init) so it's fresh on every restore.

drills.q: Is VPC attachment still a meaningful cold-start cost in 2026? What changed and when?
drills.a: No. The 2019 Hyperplane networking change replaced per-execution-environment ENI creation (10-15 seconds) with pre-created ENIs shared per subnet+security-group. VPC attachment now adds well under 50ms. The remaining real cost of VPC attachment is a NAT Gateway bill for internet egress.

drills.q: Function X is being throttled with 429s. Is this a latency problem or a capacity problem, and what two Lambda settings address it?
drills.a: A capacity problem -- concurrent executions have exceeded the account or function-level limit. Reserved concurrency sets a guaranteed floor/ceiling isolating this function from others; provisioned concurrency pre-warms environments but doesn't by itself raise the concurrency ceiling -- a quota increase may also be needed.

drills.q: An SQS-triggered Lambda has no ReportBatchItemFailures configured. One message in a batch of 10 throws an exception. What happens to the other 9?
drills.a: The entire batch of 10 becomes visible again in the queue and is retried, including the 9 that already succeeded -- their side effects can run twice unless the handler is idempotent.

drills.q: Contrast retry behavior for synchronous vs asynchronous Lambda invocation.
drills.a: Synchronous invokes are never retried by Lambda itself -- the caller (API Gateway, SDK) must implement its own retry/backoff, and a failure returns immediately. Asynchronous invokes (S3, SNS, EventBridge) are queued internally and Lambda retries automatically, by default about 2 additional attempts, invisible to whatever triggered it.

drills.q: How does memory configuration control CPU in Lambda, and what's the key number to remember?
drills.a: CPU is allocated proportionally to configured memory rather than set directly. 1,769 MB is the threshold at which a function gets one full vCPU; at the 10,240 MB max it gets roughly 6 vCPUs.

drills.q: A team doubled a function's memory to 'make it faster' and their AWS bill went up with no latency improvement. What's the likely explanation, and what should they have done instead?
drills.a: The function was I/O-bound (waiting on a downstream call), not CPU-bound, so extra CPU from the memory increase didn't reduce duration -- billing is duration x memory, so cost rose with no offsetting duration drop. They should have run AWS Lambda Power Tuning against real payloads to find the actual cost-optimal setting instead of guessing.

drills.q: Why can't you just chain Lambda self-invocations to handle a 40-minute job past the 15-minute limit?
drills.a: The 15-minute ceiling is a deliberate architectural boundary, and self-chaining produces fragile, effectively manual orchestration with no clean resumption from partial failure, no built-in state tracking between invocations, and risk of runaway recursive costs on a bug. Step Functions (bounded steps with tracked state) or Fargate/Batch (single long-running process) are the correct tools instead.

drills.q: List four scenarios where Lambda is architecturally the wrong tool even though it would technically run the workload.
drills.a: Steady high/predictable throughput (loses the cost crossover to always-on compute past a real utilization threshold); jobs needing more than 15 minutes; GPU-dependent inference (zero GPU support); and infrequently-invoked functions with large, slow-initializing dependencies where cold starts dominate perceived latency and provisioned concurrency's continuous cost isn't justified.
